items.answer: Verifiers and CSPs SHALL NOT require subscribers to change passwords periodically.

Verifiers and CSPs SHALL require passwords that are used as a single-factor authentication mechanism to be a minimum of 15 characters in length. Verifiers and CSPs MAY allow passwords that are only used as part of multi-factor authentication processes to be shorter but SHALL require them to be a minimum of eight characters in length. Verifiers and CSPs MAY allow passwords that are only used as part of multi-factor authentication processes to be shorter but SHALL require them to be a minimum of eight characters in length. Verifiers and CSPs SHOULD permit a maximum password length of at least 64 characters.
Verifiers SHALL allow the use of password managers and autofill functionality.
The salt SHALL be at least 32 bits in length and chosen to minimize salt value collisions among stored hashes (i.e., to prevent multiple subscriber accounts from having the same hashed password).
Outside parties that an organization might need to communicate with during incident handling include law enforcement, the media, vendors, and victim organizations.

Roles and responsibilities that involve cybersecurity incident response should be documented in an organization’s policies. All roles and responsibilities involving cybersecurity incident response should be documented in an organization’s policies. All appropriate individuals or parties should be designated the authority necessary to fulfill their incident response-related responsibilities.

NIST provides Implementation Examples and Informative References, which are available online and updated regularly. These resources include mappings to other incident response and cybersecurity risk management standards and guidance, as well as sources of implementation guidance that organizations can choose to utilize as needed. The resources are made publicly available on the NIST CSF website. Suggestions for new Informative References for CSF 2.0 can always be shared with NIST at olir@nist.gov. Suggestions for other resources to reference on the NIST CSF website, including additional QSG topics, should be directed to cyberframework@nist.gov.
Communication over the secondary channel SHALL use approved encryption unless sent via the public switched telephone network (PSTN).
A CSF Community Profile is typically developed for a particular sector, subsector, technology, threat type, or other use case.
The incident response life cycle is organized into three levels: Detect, Respond, and Recover, with continuous improvement indicated as the middle level.
Prioritize how quickly incident response should be performed for each incident based on its scope, likely impact, time-critical nature, and resource availability.

The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 is intended for industry, government agencies, and other organizations to manage cybersecurity risks. The CSF is valuable for any type of organization and is expected to provide appropriate guidance over a long time. The target audience for this publication includes cybersecurity program leadership, cybersecurity personnel, and others who are responsible for preparing for, detecting, responding to, or recovering from cybersecurity incidents.
